qs.q: Which pituitary hormone deficiency occurs last in progressive hypopituitarism? ---
qs.e: ACTH loss occurs last in the sequence of pituitary hormone deficiencies.

qs.q: A patient experiences a sudden severe headache, bitemporal hemianopia, and acute hypopituitarism. MRI reveals hemorrhage into a pituitary adenoma. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Pituitary apoplexy is an acute complication of a pituitary adenoma, characterized by hemorrhage or infarction within the tumor. It presents with sudden severe headache, visual disturbances (bitemporal hemianopia), ophthalmoplegia, and acute hypopituitarism, often presenting with adrenal insufficiency.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with postpartum haemorrhage now has fatigue, amenorrhoea and low blood pressure – what is the most likely diagnosis and next immediate step? — Recognise Sheehan syndrome; give stress‑dose hydrocortisone before any other therapy.

A patient with a known macroadenoma presents with new bitemporal visual loss – which investigation confirms the cause and what management follows? — Order MRI sellar; if mass effect confirmed, arrange urgent trans‑sphenoidal surgery.
How does secondary adrenal insufficiency differ from primary on laboratory testing? — Low cortisol with low ACTH versus low cortisol with high ACTH; hyperpigmentation absent in secondary.
Why must levothyroxine be delayed until after glucocorticoid replacement? — Thyroid hormone increases metabolism of cortisol, risking crisis if cortisol is insufficient.
In a HIV‑positive patient with TB meningitis, what pituitary hormone axis is most commonly affected and why? — ACTH axis, because granulomatous inflammation of the stalk impairs ACTH secretion.
Explain why a low TSH does not rule out hypothyroidism in hypopituitarism. — TSH is pituitary‑derived; pituitary failure leads to inappropriately low/normal TSH despite low thyroid hormone.

What long‑term monitoring is required after starting hormone replacement for hypopituitarism? — Check cortisol, free T4, sex steroids, IGF‑1 every 6–12 months; adjust doses based on symptoms and labs.
ai.title: Hypopituitarism
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Hypopituitarism is deficient secretion of one or more pituitary hormones, often from a pituitary lesion or infarction. In low‑resource settings, infections and postpartum haemorrhage are common causes. Diagnosis relies on clinical clues and targeted hormone tests.

b: Low cortisol with low ACTH → secondary adrenal insufficiency
Low free T4 with low/normal TSH → secondary hypothyroidism
Low IGF‑1 → growth hormone deficiency
sections.p: A state of reduced output of anterior (and sometimes posterior) pituitary hormones. Diagnosis requires at least one hormone below the age‑adjusted reference and a compatible clinical picture.

b: Partial: isolated hormone loss, often GH or gonadotropins
Pan‑hypopituitarism: cortisol, thyroid, gonadal, GH deficiency
sections.p: Classify as partial (one or two axes deficient) or pan‑hypopituitarism (≥3 axes). The Endocrine Society recommends grading by number of deficient axes and presence of acute adrenal crisis.

b: Sheehan syndrome – postpartum pituitary infarction after severe haemorrhage
Tuberculous meningitis – granulomatous infiltration of the pituitary stalk
Non‑functioning macroadenoma – mass effect, often >1 cm
Pituitary apoplexy – sudden hemorrhage into adenoma
Systemic infections (HIV, malaria) – cytokine‑mediated suppression
Autoimmune hypophysitis – more common in women, postpartum
sections.p: In East Africa, the most frequent aetiologies are vascular (Sheehan syndrome), infectious (TB meningitis, HIV‑related opportunistic infections), and space‑occupying lesions.

b: Adrenal insufficiency: weakness, nausea, postural hypotension
Secondary hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, bradycardia, dry skin
Gonadal failure: loss of libido, menstrual irregularities, infertility
GH deficiency in adults: reduced muscle mass, increased fat
Bitemporal hemianopia – suggests a large sellar mass
sections.p: Symptoms reflect the missing hormones and the underlying lesion. Look for fatigue, hypotension, hyponatraemia, cold intolerance, loss of libido, amenorrhoea, and visual field defects if a macroadenoma compresses the optic chiasm.

t.b: Is adrenal axis intact? Low cortisol with low ACTH confirms secondary adrenal insufficiency
Is thyroid axis suppressed? Low free T4 with low/normal TSH indicates secondary hypothyroidism
Elevated prolactin suggests stalk compression or prolactinoma; normal/low helps differentiate
Low IGF‑1 points to growth‑hormone deficiency; useful when GH stimulation tests are unavailable

t.a: MRI of the sellar region (if available)
t.b: Identifies adenoma, infarction, infiltrative disease; if unavailable, CT head can show large mass
Hyponatraemia may signal cortisol deficiency; hyperglycaemia can mask adrenal insufficiency

b: Acute adrenal crisis – severe hypotension, vomiting, altered mental status
Severe hyponatraemia (<125 mmol/L) – risk of seizures
Uncontrolled hypothyroidism – myxedema coma in extreme cases
sections.p: Untreated adrenal insufficiency can precipitate adrenal crisis, a life‑threatening emergency. Chronic deficiency leads to cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, and poor quality of life.

b: Glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone) – first, prevents crisis; avoid high‑dose dexamethasone if TB is present
Thyroid hormone (levothyroxine) – start only after glucocorticoids are adequate
Sex steroids (testosterone or estrogen‑progesterone) – improve libido, bone health
Growth‑hormone therapy – considered in adults with severe deficiency and reduced quality of life
Surgical removal of macroadenoma if compressive symptoms dominate; radiotherapy if surgery not feasible
sections.p: Replace deficient hormones in order of physiological urgency, treat the underlying cause, and monitor for over‑replacement.

b: Review hormone panels every 6–12 months
Provide emergency hydrocortisone injection kit
Vaccinate against infections that can precipitate crisis (influenza, pneumococcus)
Counsel on safe childbirth practices to avoid Sheehan syndrome
sections.p: Long‑term endocrine follow‑up is essential. Educate patients on stress‑dose steroids and signs of crisis. In low‑resource settings, ensure reliable supply of oral hydrocortisone and levothyroxine.

b: Addison disease – high ACTH, hyperpigmentation, often autoimmune
Primary hypothyroidism – high TSH, goitre
sections.p: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) and primary hypothyroidism can mimic parts of the picture but have high ACTH or high TSH respectively.

b: Low cortisol in severe sepsis may be stress‑related, not true deficiency
Normal TSH with low free T4 can be missed if only TSH is measured
sections.p: Acute illness can suppress cortisol and TSH, giving false‑low values. Conversely, chronic glucocorticoid therapy raises cortisol, masking secondary insufficiency.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe hypotension, vomiting, or altered consciousness – possible adrenal crisis
Rapid visual loss – suggests expanding sellar mass
